575.title: The Long Discourses, closed
575.hook: from a net that catches every view to a young man bowing in the street
575.howItsDone: In Theravada monasteries the Digha Nikaya is studied, and some of its discourses, such as the advice to Sigala, are taught to lay people as a guide for daily life.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the scene that stayed with you. Your line: yours. Today the whole collection closes, with a look at the road it took.

The first long discourse begins on a road. The Buddha and his monks are walking between two cities, and behind them walk a wandering teacher and his student, arguing. The teacher criticizes the Buddha the whole way. The student praises him the whole way. Early next morning the monks are buzzing about it, and the Buddha's first words in the whole collection are about that: if people speak against me, or against the teaching, don't get angry. If they praise us, don't get puffed up. Just say what's true and what isn't. Fifty-odd days later, this path reaches the end of that road.
screen: `TWO TRAVELERS ARGUING BEHIND.` → `NOT ANGRY, NOT PUFFED UP.` → `THE END OF THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: Look at the shape of the journey. It starts huge. In that first discourse, the Buddha lays out sixty-two views about the self and the world, and says every such theory is caught among them, like fish in a fine net cast over a small pond. Every one of them, he says, grows out of feeling and craving. It's a teaching about how minds build positions. Then come the kings, the wanderers and the gods, and the long, slow walk of the last journey to the final words. And then the collection comes down to earth. A young man named Sigala in the street at dawn, bowing to the directions because his father asked him to. The Buddha doesn't tell him to stop; he tells him what each bow could mean. Six ways money leaks. How to know a real friend. And after the four kings' protective verses, it closes with Sariputta, counting the teaching aloud so it stays whole. From the net of every view to how you treat the person who cleans your house. That's the long way home: the biggest questions end up at the kitchen table. Tomorrow a new collection begins, much shorter, with poems some scholars count among the oldest Buddhist verses.

Then let the story go quiet and rest with the breath.

576.title: The oldest poems
576.hook: among the oldest Buddhist verses, first put into English in full in 1881
576.howItsDone: Verses from the Sutta Nipata, especially the discourses on loving-kindness, blessings and the jewel, are among the texts chanted in Theravada temples and homes, and the collection is studied in monasteries.

segments.voice: Yesterday the Long Discourses closed. Your line: the long way home. Today, a new collection, and a much older sound.

In 1881, in Oxford, a volume came off the press: the tenth book in a series called the Sacred Books of the East. Inside were two Buddhist texts in English, side by side. One was the Dhammapada, translated by Max Muller. The other was a collection of poems, translated from the Pali by a Danish scholar named Viggo Fausboll. Some readers think a few of those poems belong to the oldest layers of the Buddhist canon. Today, that second book opens. Today's word: Sutta Nipata.
screen: `OXFORD, 1881.` → `A DANISH SCHOLAR'S TRANSLATION.` → `A SECOND BOOK OPENS.`

segments.voice: Sutta Nipata means something like the collection of discourses, or the gathering of suttas. It's a small book of short pieces, most of them in verse, sorted into five chapters. Some you may have met: the discourse on loving-kindness, the discourse on blessings, the rhinoceros poem. Why do some scholars call parts of it old? The language of some verses is archaic, closer to older Indian poetry. The fourth and fifth chapters, the Chapter of Eights and the Way to the Beyond, are explained line by line by another text inside the canon itself, the Niddesa. To these scholars, a commentary inside the canon suggests the poems were already old and already puzzling while the canon was still being shaped. And the life in them is spare: wanderers, forests, rivers, almost no buildings, very little organization. Some read that as a window onto the earliest days. Others are more cautious and say old verses and newer ones sit side by side. So this path reads it slowly. These are poems meant to be said aloud and remembered, with refrains that come back verse after verse, the way a song comes back to its chorus. Ahead: a snake shedding its skin, a herdsman in the rain, a rhinoceros, a plowman, a spirit with a threat, and a long list of blessings.

Say it once more, a little slower, and notice the sound in your mouth and the quiet after it, then sit with the breath.

577.title: The snake sheds its skin
577.hook: the first poem: letting go as a snake leaves its worn-out skin
577.howItsDone: The Uraga Sutta opens the Sutta Nipata and is studied and chanted in Theravada communities, and Buddhist teachers use its snake-and-skin image when they speak about letting go of anger and pride.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Sutta Nipata, and an old verse said aloud. Your line: old words. Today, the very first poem in that book, and an animal you might step back from.

Sometimes, on a hiking trail or under a porch, you find one: a snake's skin, papery, see-through, the whole length of the animal, even the scales over the eyes, turned inside out like a sock pulled off in one go. The snake is nowhere near. It rubbed its nose on a rough stone, loosened the edge, and crawled forward out of the old self it had outgrown. It didn't tear anything. It just left. The first poem of the Sutta Nipata takes that picture and repeats it, verse after verse, seventeen times.
screen: `A SKIN ON THE TRAIL.` → `INSIDE OUT, IN ONE PIECE.` → `SEVENTEEN TIMES.`

segments.voice: The poem is the Uraga Sutta. Uraga is a poetic word for snake, the one who moves on its chest. Every verse ends with the same refrain, which runs roughly: such a monk leaves behind this shore and the far shore, as a snake leaves its worn-out old skin. And every verse begins with a different thing let go, each with its own picture. The first: whoever holds back anger as it rises, the way a healer stops snake venom spreading with medicine. Another: whoever cuts off desire completely, like pulling up a lotus that grew in a pond. Another: whoever has broken down pride, the way a great flood sweeps away a flimsy bridge of reeds. And one of the strangest: whoever finds no solid core in any kind of existence, like someone searching fig trees for flowers. Those fig trees don't show their flowers; they're hidden inside the fruit. You'll look forever. Notice what the poem keeps saying about the old skin: it's worn out, already outgrown. Letting go here isn't a heroic tearing. It's leaving what no longer fits. Then the puzzle in the refrain: this shore and the far shore. Elsewhere, the far shore is the goal. Why leave that too? The old commentary offers several readings, one of them simply this world and the next. Some modern readers hear more: the one who's free doesn't cling even to having arrived. The poem doesn't explain itself. It just keeps shedding.
screen: `URAGA: THE ONE WHO MOVES ON ITS CHEST` · `ANGER, DESIRE, PRIDE, LET GO` · `THE SKIN IS ALREADY WORN OUT` · `EVEN THE FAR SHORE?` · then, large: `SHED THE OLD SKIN.`

segments.voice: Ask quietly: what am I still carrying that I've already outgrown? An old grudge, a story about yourself from ten years ago, a habit that made sense once. Don't fight it; just see that it's worn thin, like papery skin, and on the out-breath picture slipping forward out of it and leaving it on the path, knowing you can come back for it if you really need to.

578.title: Rain if you like
578.hook: a herdsman and the Buddha, on the same riverbank, both tell the sky to rain
578.carry: my hut is open, my fire is out
578.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often retell the Dhaniya poem to talk about two kinds of security, and in Theravada countries the rainy season is also when monks stay in one place for the three-month retreat.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the snake poem. Your line: shed the old skin. Today a storm is coming, and two men answer it in verse.

The weather app says heavy rain tonight. And there's a particular feeling, if you're lucky enough to have it: groceries in, laundry dry, windows shut, someone you love on the couch. Let it pour. The second poem of the Sutta Nipata starts right there, with a cattle herder named Dhaniya on the bank of the Mahi river, the monsoon clouds rolling in. He's done everything right, he's proud of it, and he sings it to the sky.
screen: `HEAVY RAIN TONIGHT.` → `DHANIYA ON THE RIVERBANK.` → `HE SINGS TO THE SKY.`

segments.voice: Dhaniya's verse goes something like this. My rice is cooked, my cows are milked. I live with my people by the river. My hut is roofed, my fire is lit. So rain if you like, sky. From nearby, another voice answers in the same rhythm. It's the Buddha, who happens to be spending one night on the same riverbank. I'm free of anger, my stubbornness is gone. I stay one night by the river. My hut is open, my fire is out. So rain if you like, sky. Hear the play on words? Dhaniya's fire is the cooking fire; the Buddha's is the fire of craving, and it's gone out. Dhaniya's roof keeps the rain away; the Buddha's hut is open, nothing to protect. They trade verses. Dhaniya: my cattle are strong, my wife is faithful, my sons are healthy. The Buddha: my raft is built, I've crossed the flood, I'm nobody's servant. Then the sky opens. A great rain falls, and Dhaniya and his wife, the poem says, go for refuge and ask to go forth. Only then does Mara join in: whoever has children delights in children; whoever has cattle delights in cattle. And the Buddha answers him: whoever has children grieves over children; whoever has cattle grieves over cattle. What people have makes them glad and makes them worry, often in the same breath. And the poem never mocks Dhaniya. His security is real. It just shows a second kind of shelter beside it.

579.title: The rhinoceros horn
579.hook: a poem whose every verse ends: wander alone like the rhinoceros horn
579.howItsDone: Buddhist monastics and lay practitioners sometimes take periods of solitary retreat, and Theravada teachers draw on the rhinoceros poem's refrain, eko care khaggavisanakappo, when they speak about solitude.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Dhaniya on the riverbank, and your line, my hut is open, my fire is out. Today, an animal that walks by itself.
screen: `MY HUT IS OPEN, MY FIRE IS OUT.`

segments.voice: The Indian rhinoceros has one horn. One. And it mostly keeps to itself, grazing through tall grass by the rivers, a huge animal that doesn't travel in a herd. In the British Library there's a birch-bark scroll, written in a language called Gandhari, which its editor dates to around the first century. It's among the oldest Buddhist manuscripts known, and one of the texts on it is a poem about that animal.
screen: `ONE HORN.` → `A BIRCH-BARK SCROLL.` → `A VERY OLD MANUSCRIPT.`

segments.voice: The poem is the third in the Sutta Nipata, the Khaggavisana Sutta, a long run of verses. Verse after verse ends with the same Pali refrain: eko care khaggavisanakappo. Wander alone, like the rhinoceros horn. Visana is a horn, and khaggavisana names the rhinoceros horn: one horn on the animal's head, one walker in the world. Some translators say like the rhinoceros, some say like its horn; the image works either way. The verses ask you to set things down. Violence toward every living being: wish harm to none. Not wishing even for a son, let alone a companion. Closeness breeds attachment, they say, and attachment breeds sorrow. Be like a deer in the forest, unbound, going wherever it wants to graze. Like a lion not startled by sounds, the wind not caught in a net, a lotus not stained by water. Is this lonely? The poem doesn't sound lonely. It sounds free. The old commentary says these verses were spoken by solitary buddhas, people who woke up on their own and lived without a community. That's the tradition's reading; the poem itself just keeps returning to the one horn. And it isn't the whole story: early on, a few verses turn a corner, and those are tomorrow's. For today, stay with the rhinoceros: steady, unhurried, needing no one's permission to walk through the grass.

segments.voice: Feel your own weight settle onto the ground, the way the rhinoceros feels the earth under it, and breathe steadily, with nobody watching and nobody needing to approve. Let each breath go the way the poem walks: not running from anyone, not looking for anyone.

580.title: Or with a friend
580.hook: in the middle of the rhinoceros poem, a door opens: if you find a wise companion, walk with them
580.carry: we praise the blessing of companionship
580.howItsDone: Buddhist teaching speaks of the kalyanamitta, the good or noble friend, and Buddhists practice in groups, with a teacher, or with a trusted companion, alongside times of solitude.

segments.voice: Yesterday: khaggavisana, the one horn, and your line, alone like the rhinoceros. Today the same poem turns a corner.

Verse after verse, the rhinoceros poem ends the same way: wander alone. Read it fast and you'd think the whole message is: don't need anyone. But look near the start. Two verses sit side by side, and they don't end the way the others do. They start with the word if. If you find someone. It's like a long letter from a friend who keeps saying I'm fine on my own, I'm fine on my own, and then, partway down the page, writes: unless you'd like to come.
screen: `VERSE AFTER VERSE: WANDER ALONE.` → `THEN, EARLY ON: IF.` → `UNLESS YOU'D LIKE TO COME.`

segments.voice: Roughly, the verse says: if you find a wise companion, a fellow traveler who lives well and is steady, walk with them, overcoming every danger, glad and mindful. And the next: if you don't find one like that, walk alone, like a king who has left a conquered kingdom behind, like an elephant alone in the forest. So solitude was never the goal. It's what you do when the right companion isn't there. The poem even says what makes a companion right. Wise: the Pali word is nipaka, skilled, discerning. Living well. Steady. Someone who makes the dangers smaller, not bigger. A little later comes a line like a proverb: we praise the blessing of companionship. Keep company with those better than you or equal to you. If you can't find them, live blamelessly and walk alone. Elsewhere in the discourses, Ananda, the Buddha's attendant, says: good friendship is half of the spiritual life. And the Buddha corrects him: don't say that, Ananda. Good friendship is the whole of the spiritual life. So the tradition holds both, the one horn and the good friend. Not a contradiction: two pictures of the same freedom. You don't need a crowd. And when someone wise and kind turns up on your road, you don't need to walk alone either.

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who makes the road safer, wise, steady and kind, near or far or no longer living, and picture walking beside them, matching steps, not talking much. 581.title: Faith the seed
581.hook: a brahmin farmer with five hundred plows tells the Buddha to plow for his food
581.carry: plant one seed you can't see
581.howItsDone: Theravada monastics live on alms and do not farm or handle money; lay supporters offer food, and the Kasibharadvaja poem is one text teachers use to explain how monastic and lay life support each other.

segments.voice: Yesterday: sahaya, the wise companion, and your line, we praise the blessing of companionship. Today ends the week, out in a field at sowing time.

Sowing day on a big farm in Magadha. A brahmin named Kasi Bharadvaja has five hundred plows out in his fields, and at lunchtime he's handing out food to the workers. A man with a bowl walks up and stands quietly at the edge of the line. The farmer isn't impressed. I plow and I sow, he says, and then I eat. You should plow and sow too, and then you can eat. It's a fair point, the kind people still make about anyone whose work you can't see. The Buddha's answer is today's poem.
screen: `FIVE HUNDRED PLOWS AT SOWING TIME.` → `I PLOW, THEN I EAT.` → `YOU SHOULD TOO.`

segments.voice: The Buddha says: I plow and sow too, brahmin, and then I eat. The farmer is puzzled: we don't see your yoke, your plow, your oxen. So the Buddha describes his farm, in verse. Faith is the seed. Discipline is the rain. Wisdom is my yoke and plow. Conscience is the pole, the mind the strap, mindfulness my plowshare and goad. Guarded in body and speech, moderate in food. Truth is how I weed. Effort is my ox, pulling toward freedom without turning back. And this plowing has the deathless as its harvest. Notice where faith sits: it's the seed, the very first thing, put into the ground before anything shows. Saddha, the Pali word, can be translated faith, trust or confidence. Here it isn't the harvest. It's the trust that gets you to begin. Then wisdom and effort and mindfulness do the work. The farmer is moved and offers milk-rice in a bronze bowl. The Buddha declines: food given in payment for verses isn't for him. In the end the farmer asks to go forth. That closes the week, too. A whole collection closed, the oldest poems opened: a snake shedding its skin, a herdsman in the rain, a rhinoceros alone, a friend on the road, and now a field. Each sets an ordinary picture beside a deeper one.
screen: `I PLOW AND SOW TOO` · `FAITH THE SEED, WISDOM THE PLOW` · `TRUST THAT GETS YOU TO BEGIN` · `A WEEK OF ORDINARY PICTURES` · then, large: `FAITH THE SEED.`

segments.voice: Quietly name your own farm: your seed, the small trust that got you started on something good; your plow, the steady tool you use, like patience, honesty or an early alarm; your ox, the effort that keeps pulling. Then let the breath be the slow work of a field, nothing to force, just showing up.
saddha. The Buddha's farming poem: trust is the seed you plant first, then wisdom plows, effort pulls, and the harvest is freedom. Today's word.
Your line: plant one seed you can't see. Trust starts it; wisdom and effort grow it. See you tomorrow.

original.note: Pali saddha: faith, trust, confidence. in Sn 1.4, the seed.

what a scholar hears: saddha is also rendered confidence; some early texts link it to a teacher one has tested, and the Kasibharadvaja Sutta appears in both the Sutta Nipata and the Samyutta Nikaya.

chat.says: In that farming poem, where does faith fit in?
options: It's the seed: the trust you plant first, then wisdom and effort work.
It's the harvest: the reward that comes at the very end of the path.
It's the rain: what falls on the field once the plowing is all done.
chat.meaning: In the Buddha's farming poem faith is the seed, planted first. Wisdom is the plow, effort the ox, and the harvest is the deathless.
